title: Booked to Wait
passage:
The mate on the first sailing has taken to carrying a paperback. He reads it at the Brackenhithe slip with the ramp down and the engines turning, because the boat is now booked to sit there. In 2005 the crossing to the north shore was printed as eighteen minutes. This year it is printed as twenty-seven. The water is the same width it always was. Since 2011 the operator has earned a quality payment in any quarter when at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute, and has taken it in twenty-three of the last twenty-four quarters. The published reliability figure stood at seventy-one per cent in 2005. Last year it was ninety-six. By the only measure the contract knows, the crossing has never run better.

Kathleen Cattermay, a transport analyst working on contract, was asked by the county’s scrutiny committee for something narrow. She went at it from the passenger’s end. Every ticketed vehicle at Brackenhithe is stamped twice, at the barrier on the slip and at the ramp on the far side. She has those stamps going back to 2012. The median time from barrier to far ramp has gone from thirty-nine minutes to fifty-four. The booked crossing sets the length of a round trip, the round trip sets how many departures fit into a day, and a passenger waits for a departure, not a boat. Add nine minutes at each end and you lose a sailing, and the lost sailing costs everyone not on it far more than the nine minutes cost the boat. “The measurement I will defend,” she says. “How much of the gap belongs to the timetable is the weaker half of it. Something else happened in the middle of my series.”

Trevor Cottam has run operations for the company for eleven years and says the something else is nearly the whole of it. He starts with 2005. The median crossing that year took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking. In his reading the old seventy-one per cent measured a promise nobody could keep, and five of the nine added minutes only brought the book level with the boat. Then there is work that really has got longer. The linkspan – the hinged ramp the vehicles drive over – was rebuilt in 2013 for heavier axle loads, and its locking sequence takes a manufacturer’s ninety seconds at each berth. And in 2016 the relief boat’s passenger certificate ran out and the company did not replace her. “Two boats and the old book gave you a departure every twenty-five minutes,” Cottam says. “One boat gives you one every seventy. Pad the book by nothing at all and you would still have that.”

Alison Bexwarden drafted the punctuality clause for the transport authority in 2011 and does not accept that it caused any of this. In the consultation that preceded it, sixty-one per cent of those answering ranked knowing when the boat would go above getting across sooner. The clause measures what people asked to have measured. She will concede the shape of the incentive: an operator publishes a year ahead and is penalised for altering the book inside a year, so a contract of that shape produces a cautious book. What she volunteers is something nobody asks her about. A sailing that does not run is not late; it leaves the count altogether. In the first quarter of 2023 the crossing lost forty-one sailings to weather and a gearbox, and its reliability figure was ninety-seven per cent, the highest it had ever been. “That is the line I would change,” she says, “and nobody writes to me about it.”

Nobody disputes the stamps. Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and does not contest the fifteen minutes. Where Cattermay’s case thins is the join. Her thirteen years hold the linkspan work, the padding and the loss of the relief boat, and she says herself that she cannot pull them apart. Until somebody can, the timetable is an explanation that fits without having been tested. Cottam’s account has a soft place in the same decade. The book went from eighteen minutes to twenty-four in 2013, three years before the certificate ran out, and the interval between departures went from twenty-five minutes to thirty-two. Some of the frequency was gone before the boat was. The ninety seconds is a manufacturer’s figure; nobody has timed it on the linkspan. None of the three is arguing about the sentence Bexwarden raised herself. The service goes out to tender in the spring. The draft that went to the harbour board in July carries the 2011 clause word for word, including the line about cancelled sailings.
– Julian Dowlesham

questions.prompt: What are we told about the quality payment in the operator’s contract?

options.text: It is paid only in quarters when every sailing berths exactly on schedule.
It was written into the contract when the second boat was withdrawn.
It turns on how many sailings berth inside the margin the contract sets.
It is reduced, though not withdrawn, in quarters when sailings are cancelled.

questions.rationale: KEY C. Paragraph 1 states the clause: the operator earns the quality payment in any quarter when at least ninety-two per cent of its sailings berth within ten minutes of the booked minute. C paraphrases that as a proportion measured against the margin the contract sets, without reusing the passage's wording. A is a QUANTIFIER UPGRADE on two axes at once - the threshold (ninety-two per cent becomes 'every sailing') and the tolerance (ten minutes becomes 'exactly on schedule'); it tempts because it is the shape a reader expects a punctuality rule to have. B is a WRONG-LOCATION splice: both facts are in the text (the clause dates from 2011, the relief boat went in 2016) but the text never joins them, and the five-year gap refutes the join. D is an OUTSIDE-KNOWLEDGE trap, and the strongest one here, because real performance regimes usually do dock an operator for cancellations; paragraph 4 says the opposite, that a sailing which does not run leaves the count altogether, so the payment is neither reduced nor withheld. D is also the most qualified-sounding option in the set ('though not withdrawn'), which is deliberate: the hedge-picking heuristic lands on a distractor here.

questions.prompt: What does Cottam say about the 2005 timetable?

options.text: The crossing was already taking longer than the printed time allowed.
Every sailing that year arrived later than the timetable promised.
It was broadly realistic except in the worst of the winter weather.
It was written before anyone was measuring how late the boat was.

questions.rationale: KEY A. In paragraph 3 Cottam's first move is that the median crossing in 2005 took twenty-four minutes against an eighteen-minute booking, so the boat was already over the printed time before any minutes were added; A restates that in different words. B is the QUANTIFIER UPGRADE the item is built for: a median is not every sailing, and 'every sailing ... arrived later' converts a central tendency into a universal. C is a HEDGED DISTRACTOR with no support - 'broadly realistic except in the worst of the winter weather' sounds like the careful answer and is exactly the reading Cottam rejects; this is the unit's second break of the correct-equals-qualified correlation. D is a WRONG-LOCATION inference that a skimmer reaches by dating measurement to the 2011 clause; paragraph 1 gives a published reliability figure for 2005, so somebody was measuring six years earlier.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the withdrawal of the relief boat?

options.text: The company sold it once its certificate had expired.
The company let it go in order to lengthen the gaps between sailings.
Nothing that has happened to the queues since can be blamed on the timetable.
Losing it took more departures out of the day than the timetable changes had.

questions.rationale: KEY D. This is a one-inch inference from arithmetic the text supplies but never adds up. Cottam says two boats and the old book gave a departure every twenty-five minutes and one boat gives one every seventy; paragraph 5 says the interval had already gone from twenty-five to thirty-two under the 2013 book, three years before the certificate ran out. So the timetable accounts for about seven minutes of that interval and the lost boat for about thirty-eight: losing the boat took more departures out of the day than the padding did. A is the TOO-LITERAL trap with an actor-level distortion - the text says the certificate ran out and the company did not replace her, and says nothing about a sale, so A is retrieval that has been nudged off the facts. B is a TWO-STEP LEAP that also reverses the arrow: longer gaps are a consequence of running one boat, not a motive for withdrawing the second. C is an OVERGENERALISATION of Cottam's position into an absolute ('Nothing ... can be blamed on the timetable'), which paragraph 5 refutes in his own case.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude towards Cattermay’s argument?

options.text: He is persuaded by Cottam and considers the question settled in the operator’s favour.
He accepts her numbers but not the cause she assigns them.
He treats it as an argument the evidence cannot support at all.
He lays the positions out and keeps his own judgement off the page.

questions.rationale: KEY B. Paragraph 5 is the writer's verdict and it splits: nobody disputes the stamps, Cottam has accepted the barrier series in writing, and what thins is the join - her thirteen years hold the linkspan work, the padding and the loss of the relief boat together, so the timetable is an explanation that fits without having been tested. B states that division: her numbers stand, the cause she assigns them does not. A is the ROLE-OR-ATTRIBUTION SWAP that is this family's signature: it hands the writer the operator's position, and paragraph 5 refuses it by naming a soft place in Cottam's own account. C is a POLARITY OVERSHOOT - 'the evidence cannot support at all' is dismissal, where the text says the explanation fits the evidence but has not been tested by it. D is the NEUTRAL-REPORTER misread, defensible only if paragraph 5 is skipped, since the writer there judges both principals and names what neither is arguing about.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The condition of the ramp at Brackenhithe and what its rebuilding cost the service.
How ferry services on estuaries across the country have been run down since 2005.
The difficulty of drawing firm conclusions from thirteen years of ticket data.
A rising reliability figure, a slower journey, and a quarrel over what connects them.

questions.rationale: KEY D. The whole-text shape is a reliability figure that has risen from seventy-one to ninety-six per cent while the median barrier-to-ramp time has risen from thirty-nine minutes to fifty-four, and a three-way argument about what joins those two movements. D names all three parts without settling the argument, which is what the text does. A is a SCOPE ERROR that promotes a paragraph-3 sub-point, the rebuilt linkspan, to the subject of the piece. B is the TOO-BROAD theme: the text is about one crossing under one contract and never generalises to ferry services elsewhere, so B is a title-plausible claim the passage does not argue. C is the CAUTIOUS-SOUNDING scope error, and it is placed here on purpose - it is the option a hedge-picking solver reaches for, it borrows the genuine limitation the writer states, and it still mistakes a difficulty inside the argument for the subject of the argument.
